column5: wind weight and waters by measure
column6: The commentary defines qaddara as making quantity manifest and extends it to rain and the created order; Job says God gives the wind a weight and apportions the waters by measure, matching both material elements.

column5: all things by measure, number, and weight
column6: The commentary makes the verbs objectless so that measure reaches every created thing; Wisdom describes the Creator's ordering of all things by measure, number, and weight, an unusually exact cosmological counterpart.

column5: decree for rain and path for lightning
column6: The page says rain descends in a specified measure and that divine measure governs a creature's course; Job joins God's decree for rain to a path for the thunderbolt in its account of creation's ordering.

column5: numbered days and uncrossable boundary
column6: The commentary insists that qadar includes a thing's term and endpoint; Job speaks of a human whose days and months are numbered by God and whose boundary cannot be passed.

column5: fixed number of human days
column6: The commentary applies measure to a creature's allotted duration; Sirach gives human beings a fixed number of days while granting them earthly authority, a close formulation of duration within creaturely limits.

column5: allotted periods and habitation boundaries
column6: The commentary universalizes divine measuring as a limit and destination for every being; Paul's Areopagus speech says God determined nations' allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling places.

column5: luminaries for seasons, days, and years
column6: The commentary treats sun and moon as measured bodies whose courses disclose time; Genesis assigns the lights signs, appointed seasons, days, and years in the ordered creation account.

column5: moon for seasons and sun's setting
column6: The commentary reads the moon's stations and return as a measured life-cycle; this psalm gives the moon its role in marking seasons and says the sun knows its setting.

column5: heavenly host brought out by number
column6: The commentary uses calculated stars to display a measured cosmos; Isaiah portrays God bringing out the heavenly host by number and calling each one by name, with none missing.

column5: grass withers under God's breath
column6: The commentary joins the pasture's emergence to its eventual blackening and decay; Isaiah's grass withers and flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it.

column5: all flesh as grass that withers
column6: The page makes vegetation's end a figure for creaturely limits; 1 Peter takes up the grass-and-fading-flower image for mortal flesh, extending the same movement from growth to transience.

column5: migrating birds know their appointed times
column6: The commentary contrasts the bee's divinely fitted path with people who refuse shown guidance; Jeremiah's stork, dove, swift, and crane keep their appointed migrations while the people do not know the LORD's ordinance.

column5: continual guidance and provision in dry places
column6: The commentary binds guidance to measured provision rather than humiliation; Isaiah promises that the LORD will guide continually, satisfy need in parched places, and make the recipient like a watered garden.

column5: God teaches benefit and leads the proper way
column6: The commentary says guidance is the Creator's purposive leading, not mere direction at a distance; Isaiah names the LORD as the one who teaches for benefit and leads people in the way they should go.

column5: green pastures and restful waters
column6: The commentary places divine guidance beside the pasture that follows in 87:4 and develops a flock image; the psalm's shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them beside waters of rest.

column5: guidance in right paths
column6: The commentary distinguishes being shown the way from the traveler's following it; Psalm 23 has the shepherd restore the life of the sheep and guide it in right paths for his name's sake.

column5: shepherd's leading into pasture
column6: The commentary's guide goes before a flock toward grazing; Ezekiel's divine shepherd brings the scattered sheep into their land and feeds them on Israel's mountains, watercourses, and inhabited places.

column5: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
column6: The commentary explains hidayet through the guide's physical precedence over the herd; Jesus' shepherd leads his own sheep out, goes ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice.

column5: shepherd guiding to springs of water
column6: The commentary moves from a leading shepherd to the pasture's nourishment; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherding and guiding the faithful to springs of the water of life.

column5: pillar of fire going before Israel
column6: The commentary's guide is an ahead-going presence and Musa finds guidance at fire; Exodus says the LORD goes before Israel in cloud by day and fire by night in order to lead them on the way.

column5: Moses shepherding at Horeb
column6: The commentary lingers over staff, flock, wilderness journey, and the fire-scene of Moses; Exodus introduces him while leading Jethro's flock beyond the wilderness to Horeb.

column5: fire in the bush at Moses' call
column6: The commentary has the lost traveler see a distant fire and receive a different, divine guidance there; Exodus likewise makes flame in a bush the immediate setting of Moses' divine encounter.

column5: divine presence with commissioned Moses
column6: Musa says at the sea that his Lord is with him and will guide him; at the bush God answers Moses' reluctance with the promise, in its commissioning context, that God will be with him.

column5: staff raised and sea divided
column6: The commentary pairs Musa's expectation of imminent guidance with the command to strike the sea using his staff; Exodus directs Moses to lift his staff so the sea will divide and Israel can pass through.

column5: Moses flees Pharaoh to Midian
column6: The commentary recounts Musa's fearful departure from the city and journey toward Midian while asking for the straight way; Exodus has Pharaoh seek his life and Moses flee to dwell in Midian.

column5: Pharaoh's question becomes refusal to obey
column6: The commentary makes Pharaoh's question about the Lord elicit Musa's account of the creator who gives form and guidance; Exodus frames Pharaoh's question as a refusal to know the LORD, obey his voice, or release Israel.

column5: Wisdom leads through the Red Sea
column6: The commentary reads the divided sea as the answer to Musa's trust that God will guide; Wisdom of Solomon retells the crossing as Wisdom leading the people through deep water, a Jewish interpretive recasting of the route.

column5: Red Sea crossing interpreted as faith
column6: The commentary stresses a divinely opened way at the sea; Hebrews says the people passed through the Red Sea by faith while the Egyptians were overwhelmed, adding a Christian account of the travelers' response.

column5: Abraham shown an unknown land
column6: The commentary sets Ibrahim's claim that the Creator guides him beside a journey whose destination lies ahead; Genesis calls Abram to leave his country for a land that God will show him.

column5: Abraham obeys without knowing destination
column6: The commentary turns Abraham's creation-and-guidance confession into an ongoing personal journey; Hebrews interprets his departure as obedient travel toward an inheritance, even though he did not know where he was going.

column5: Moses asks to know God's ways
column6: The commentary ends in the worshiper's request to be guided on a straight path and ties it to Musa; Moses asks God to make God's ways known so that he may know God and find favor.

column5: formed body and divinely given life
column6: The commentary reads qaddara alongside creation and the fitted human body; Genesis forms the human from ground and gives life by divine breath, a foundational formation scene beside that claim.

column5: formed in the womb and appointed
column6: The commentary develops measurement as a body's formation and a life's destined direction; Jeremiah is known, consecrated, and appointed before God forms him in the womb.

column5: body formed from seed over ten months
column6: The commentary fills the unspoken object with the human made from a drop and held for an appointed term; Wisdom of Solomon describes its speaker as molded in the womb from human seed over a stated period.

column5: pre-birth decree and moral exception
column6: The commentary separates a creature's given measure from the traveler's responsibility to follow guidance; this rabbinic passage assigns strength, wealth, and similar traits before birth but explicitly does not decree righteousness or wickedness.

column5: measured manna leaves neither surplus nor lack
column6: The commentary says restricted provision is a fitting measure rather than disgrace; at the manna gathering, whoever gathered much had no surplus and whoever gathered little had no lack.

column5: food apportioned as one's due
column6: The commentary rejects reading constrained provision as divine contempt and calls it a measure; the prayer in Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches but for the food apportioned to the speaker.

column5: gift accepted according to what one has
column6: The commentary cites the command to spend from what God has given and not be loaded beyond it; Paul makes a contribution acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what is absent.

column5: just balances, weights, and measures
column6: The commentary contrasts human calculation with the God-given balance by which it should be judged; Leviticus commands just balances, weights, ephah, and hin under the authority of the liberating LORD.

column5: human planning and God-directed steps
column6: The commentary says people may think and measure but wrongly replace the shown way with their own; Proverbs permits a person to plan a path while assigning the establishment of actual steps to the LORD.

column5: a walker's steps are not self-directed
column6: The commentary makes human calculation answerable to the guidance that belongs to God; Jeremiah confesses that a person's way is not self-owned and that a walker cannot direct his own steps.

column5: voice saying this is the way
column6: The commentary defines guidance as concretely showing a road while leaving the traveler to take it; Isaiah imagines a voice behind the people saying, This is the way, walk in it.

column5: good path offered and refused
column6: The commentary says the same shown way divides those who accept the reminder from those who pass by it; Jeremiah calls for the ancient good path and records the people's answer, We will not walk in it.

column5: life and death set before human choice
column6: The commentary pairs complete divine guidance with the traveler's non-coerced choice; Deuteronomy places life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and commands them to choose life.

column5: creation and free choice
column6: The commentary insists that hidayet is not forced dragging; Sirach says God created human beings and left them in the power of their own free choice.

column5: life or death given according to choice
column6: The commentary's two ways issue in divergent outcomes while remaining a choice; Sirach puts life and death before each person and says whichever is chosen will be given.

column5: foreknowledge and freedom of choice
column6: The commentary holds divine measure and guidance together with real human following or refusal; Avot's compact maxim says that everything is foreseen while freedom of choice is granted.

column5: all in Heaven's hands except fear
column6: The commentary assigns guidance to the Lord but response to the traveler who fears or turns away; the Talmud's maxim reserves fear of Heaven as the stated exception to what lies in Heaven's hands.

column5: the two ways of life and death
column6: The commentary explicitly frames the shown road as two possible courses whose outcome depends on walking them; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.

column5: broad way leading to destruction
column6: The commentary says one person follows the shown way while another moves aside from it; Jesus' warning identifies a broad gate and way whose many travelers reach destruction.

column5: narrow way leading to life
column6: The commentary's alternative to passing by guidance is a way actually taken toward a good end; Jesus names the narrow gate and constricted way that leads to life and is found by few.

column5: divine gathering refused by its hearers
column6: The commentary rejects an account of guidance as coercion and describes people who decline its reminder; Jesus says he wished to gather Jerusalem's children but they were unwilling.

column5: cords of kindness and food
column6: The commentary defines hidayet as gentle leading and links it to nourishment rather than force; Hosea pictures God drawing Israel with human cords and bands of love, then bending down to feed them.

column5: gentle shepherding of the flock
column6: The commentary's guide is both a flock's leader and a companion attentive to weakness; Isaiah's shepherd gathers lambs, carries them close, and gently leads those with young.

column5: star going before travelers to a destination
column6: The commentary says measured heavenly bodies guide land and sea travelers, though they themselves set; Matthew's star goes before the Magi and stops over the place they are seeking.

column5: light guiding feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary develops guidance through fire, light, and a travelled way; Zechariah's song says the dawn from on high gives light in darkness and guides feet into the way of peace.

column5: need for a guide to understand the way
column6: The commentary calls a guide one who makes a road and destination known and then shows the guided person becoming a leader; the Ethiopian asks Philip how he can understand Scripture unless someone guides him.

column5: courses, dominions, and seasons of luminaries
column6: The commentary works through the measured movements of sun, moon, and stars; the opening of the Astronomical Book introduces the luminaries by their courses, dominions, seasons, names, and origins.

column5: moon marking festivals and completing its course
column6: The commentary's moon reaches measured stations and wanes at its limit; Sirach makes the moon a sign for festal times and describes its light waning when its course is complete.

column5: each blade of grass commanded to grow
column6: The commentary moves from God measuring and guiding all things to the pasture's emergence; this midrash imagines every blade of grass as receiving a heavenly directive to grow, a Jewish reading of creaturely guidance.

column5: angel sent ahead for the bride journey
column6: The commentary explains hidayet through an ahead-going guide and through bringing a bride to her husband; Abraham says God will send an angel before his servant so a wife can be brought for Isaac.

column5: sacrifice taken to a divinely shown place
column6: The commentary's sacrificial animal is defined by reaching its appointed sacred destination; Genesis sends Abraham with an offering to a mountain God will show, a related destination-bound sacrifice without equating the rites.

column5: rain, childbirth, and resurrection as divine keys
column6: The commentary joins measured rain, formation in the womb, and the end that reaches resurrection; this Talmudic triad treats rain, childbirth, and revival of the dead as keys retained by God.

column5: testing bounded by ability and an escape way
column6: The commentary says divine measure bounds a person's burden and opens a way after hardship; Paul says testing will not exceed ability and that God provides the way out so it can be endured.

column5: traveler's prayer for steps directed in peace
column6: The commentary turns the general report that God guides into the worshiper's own request for a path; the Talmud's travel prayer asks God to lead the traveler and direct the steps in peace.

column5: Eden's way guarded after expulsion
column6: The commentary reads Adam's descent as followed by a promised guidance that can be followed without error or misery; Genesis ends its expulsion scene by guarding the way to the tree of life with cherubim and a flaming sword.

column5: prenatal Torah followed by forgetting at birth
column6: The commentary joins womb-formation to the surah's promise that the Prophet will be made to recite and not forget; this Talmudic birth tradition has the embryo taught Torah and then made to forget it at birth.

column5: Spirit teaches and brings words to remembrance
column6: The commentary makes non-forgetting the sequel to the creator's guidance and ties it to revelation; John says the Paraclete will teach the disciples all things and bring Jesus' words to their remembrance.

column5: easy yoke and light burden
column6: The commentary connects measured provision and guided travel with the promise of ease after hardship; Jesus characterizes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, a focused Christian counterpart to that eased way.

column5: God's summons and human freedom
column6: The commentary reads the difference between guidance and following as a protection against coercion; Irenaeus uses Christ's lament over unwilling Jerusalem to argue that God made human beings free to obey or refuse.

column5: David rejects Saul's untested armor
column6: The commentary makes David's well-measured armor a divinely taught craft whose parts must fit; in the biblical David-and-armor scene, David removes Saul's untested gear because he cannot walk in it, giving a pointedly different emphasis.

column5: forty years before the flame at Sinai
column6: The commentary calls Musa's arrival after years in Midian a coming at an appointed measure and places the call at fire; Stephen's speech similarly puts the flame in the Sinai wilderness after forty years, supplying a Christian chronological framing.
